stem: A frequency distribution uses inclusive class intervals: 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49. To convert these to exclusive (continuous) class boundaries, a correction factor equal to half the gap between classes is subtracted from the lower limit and added to the upper limit. The lower class boundary of the class 20-29 is:

per_option_rationale.rationale: Gap between consecutive classes = 20 - 19 = 1. Correction factor = 1/2 = 0.5. Lower boundary of 20-29 = 20 - 0.5 = 19.5.
Taking the lower limit as-is without applying any boundary correction, treating inclusive limits as boundaries directly.
Adding 0.5 to the lower limit (20 + 0.5 = 20.5) instead of subtracting it.
Subtracting 1.5 instead of 0.5 from the lower limit, giving 20 - 1.5 = 18.5.

explanation: For inclusive class intervals, the gap between consecutive upper limit and next lower limit = 20 - 19 = 1. Correction factor = 0.5. Lower class boundary = lower class limit - 0.5 = 20 - 0.5 = 19.5.

explanation_sections.approach: Identify the model: inclusive to exclusive boundary conversion. Recipe: (1) find the gap between consecutive classes: upper limit of one class (19) to lower limit of next class (20), gap = 1; (2) correction factor = gap/2 = 0.5; (3) lower boundary = lower limit - correction = 20 - 0.5 = 19.5.
explanation_sections.lesson: When class intervals are inclusive (e.g. 10-19, 20-29), the class boundary is obtained by subtracting 0.5 from the lower limit and adding 0.5 to the upper limit, assuming unit-scale data.
explanation_sections.timing: 30 seconds. Identify gap = 1, halve to 0.5, subtract from lower limit. Trap: option 3 (20.5) adds instead of subtracts.
